I think the nature of deep learning is going to make standardizing the technology very difficult. Deep learning essentially learns from data. That has two important implications. The first is that the software will never be done per se - it will always be learning and improving itself. The second is that the software itself would be relatively useless. What matters is the data that the software trains itself on. I do think we'll see open standards to enable things like self driving vehicles to communicate with one another to increase efficiency and safety, but I'd expect actual implementations to remain proprietary with the most successful company likely turning licensing their software into a major industry itself.

Two self driving vehicles won't just randomly crash into each other. There would need to be extenuating circumstances and companies are going out of their way to minimize the possibilities of these circumstances so much as possible. For instance something that Tesla did in this case is have redundancy for systems. We know the accelerator didn't fail since there are actually two redundant gauges for acceleration. The computer only propagates the signal for acceleration if both gauges independently detect the input for acceleration - or pressing on the 'gas' pedal. Funny sound name for a pure electric vehicle! The chance of any given piece of hardware failing is incredibly low. The chance of two specific pieces of hardware in the same vehicle simultaneously failing is basically 0. Going back to Volvo they've stated they will be installing similar redundant systems for nearly every critical piece of hardware in the vehicle. In cases of something like extremely bad weather where there is no clear individual at fault I'm not sure. A reasonable result seems to be for both companies to share responsibility and cover the repair costs of their drivers' vehicles. It's going to be extremely rare in any case.

As for how will we know they'll take responsibility. What Volvo is saying cannot be just marketing speak. In the US we're only required to have liability insurance. If Volvo is willing to take liability for any crashes caused that means you no longer need to purchase insurance for a self-driving only Volvo vehicle. And in fact they would actually be offering something closer to full-coverage than liability insurance. That has major legal implications and assuming they stick to it will require legal changes and certainly amount to more than, "... but you promised!"
